title: The Global Health Revolution: Progress, Inequality, and the Challenges Ahead
paragraphs: Over the past two centuries, humanity has achieved extraordinary progress in health and medicine. Average global life expectancy has more than doubled — from around 35 years in 1800 to over 72 years today. Infant mortality has fallen dramatically. Diseases that once killed millions, including smallpox and polio, have been eliminated or nearly eradicated through vaccination campaigns. Surgical techniques, antibiotics, and diagnostic technology have transformed what it means to be ill. By almost any measure, the average person alive today is healthier, and lives longer, than at almost any previous point in history.

This progress is unevenly distributed, however. A child born in a high-income country can expect to live, on average, eighteen years longer than a child born in a low-income country. In wealthy nations, healthcare systems provide access to advanced treatments, early screening, and preventive care. In many low- and middle-income countries, basic healthcare is limited by a shortage of trained medical professionals, insufficient funding, and inadequate infrastructure. Preventable diseases — those that could be treated or avoided with basic medicine — remain leading causes of death in some of the world's poorest regions.

Communicable diseases — those that spread from person to person, such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS — continue to impose an enormous burden on global health, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia. Alongside these, non-communicable diseases — conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, cancer, and chronic respiratory illness — are now the leading causes of death globally, including in many middle-income countries. This "double burden" of communicable and non-communicable disease places enormous pressure on health systems that were often designed to address only one or the other.

One of the most significant developments in modern medicine is the shift from treating illness to preventing it. Preventive medicine — the practice of identifying and addressing risk factors before disease develops — has been shown to be both more effective and more cost-efficient than treatment after the fact. Vaccination, regular health screening, public health campaigns about diet, exercise, and smoking cessation, and the management of chronic conditions such as hypertension before they cause catastrophic events like strokes or heart attacks, all fall within the domain of preventive medicine.

The COVID-19 pandemic, which emerged in 2019 and spread globally within months, provided a dramatic demonstration of both the strengths and the vulnerabilities of modern global health systems. The development of effective vaccines within a year was a remarkable scientific achievement, drawing on decades of prior research into mRNA technology. At the same time, the pandemic exposed deep inequalities in vaccine distribution, healthcare capacity, and public health communication. Countries with weaker health systems and less economic resilience suffered disproportionately — a pattern that reflected broader global inequalities.

Digital health technologies represent one of the most promising frontiers in twenty-first-century medicine. Wearable devices that monitor heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep patterns are already providing individuals with data that was previously available only in clinical settings. Artificial intelligence is being applied to diagnostic imaging, drug discovery, and personalised treatment plans. Telemedicine — the delivery of healthcare remotely via digital platforms — has expanded access to medical consultation for people in rural or underserved areas. The potential for technology to democratise access to high-quality healthcare is real, though it depends on addressing the digital divide.

The future of global health will be shaped by how well humanity addresses the interaction between environmental, social, and biological factors. Climate change is already affecting patterns of disease — expanding the geographic range of mosquito-borne illnesses, increasing the frequency of heat-related deaths, and threatening food and water security. Social determinants — income, education, housing, and working conditions — account for a large proportion of health outcomes. A truly healthy society is not just one with good hospitals; it is one that addresses the conditions that keep people well in the first place.

vocab.example: "Smallpox was eradicated through a global vaccination campaign."

task1Items.correct: It has more than doubled — from around 35 years in 1800 to over 72 years today

task1Items.question: What is the "double burden of disease"?
task1Items.correct: The coexistence of communicable and non-communicable diseases in the same population

task1Items.question: What is preventive medicine and why is it important?
task1Items.correct: Identifying and addressing risk factors before disease develops — more effective and cost-efficient than treatment

task1Items.question: What did the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate about global health?
task1Items.correct: Both the strengths (rapid vaccine development) and vulnerabilities (inequalities in distribution and capacity)

task1Items.question: What are "social determinants of health"?
task1Items.correct: Non-medical factors like income, education, housing, and working conditions that influence health outcomes
